lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- What Should I Do?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Cristiane Gomes de Moura | Lesson 9 -- What Should I Do?
lesson.grammar_point: modals for advice and possibility -- should and shouldn't, could for options, might for what is only possible

listenings.text: The best advice I ever got, I ignored for four years. A woman I barely knew told me I should stop asking people whether I was ready, because nobody was ever going to say yes, and because the question was the wrong one. I said thank you, and carried on asking. I asked my sister. I asked my old boss. I asked a man on a plane who had no idea what I was talking about. Everybody gave me a different answer, and every single one of them started with the same two words. It depends. Four years later I did the thing anyway, badly, and it was fine. So now, when somebody asks me whether they should do it, I do not say yes and I do not say no. I say: you should stop asking. If you are still asking after two months, you already know the answer, and what you are really looking for is somebody to blame if it goes wrong.

I want to defend the phrase people hate most in English, which is: it depends. It sounds like somebody who will not commit. Usually it is the opposite. Should you take the job? It depends on whether you can afford six months of being bad at it. Should you tell your boss what you actually think? It depends on what she did the last time somebody told her something she did not want to hear. Should you move to another city? It depends on how many people you know there, and on how quickly you make friends, which is a thing you already know about yourself. Every one of those is a real question with a real answer. The person saying it depends is handing you the questions. Anybody who answers with just a yes or just a no is either not listening, or has stopped being careful.

There is a difference between a bad decision and a mistake, and almost nobody keeps them apart. A mistake is when you had the information and you did not use it. A bad decision is when you did not have the information, you chose anyway, and it went badly, which is most of life. If you only call something a mistake after you see how it ended, then every decision is a coin, and you will spend the rest of your life frightened of choosing. So the useful question is not: was I right? The useful question is: with what I knew that Tuesday, is that still the choice I would make? If the answer is yes, it was not a mistake. It was a risk, you took it with your eyes open, and it did not work. Those are different things, and only one of them is worth losing sleep over.
